strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple base models (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeQwen, Qwen2.5-Coder), multiple benchmarks (VerilogEval Machine/Human, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0), and multiple metric families (functional correctness and PPA), providing broad evidence of the method's effectiveness.

The hierarchical/gated reward design (Syntax→Function→Synthesis→PPA) is a sensible engineering solution to avoid wasting expensive EDA calls on invalid designs, and the paper provides a clear ablation (Table 4) showing each reward component contributes to final performance.

CDPO is compared directly against GRPO and DAPO baselines (Table 5, Figure 8/9) under matched training conditions, giving reasonably controlled evidence that curriculum weighting and advantage-level (rather than reward-level) aggregation help stabilize multi-objective optimization.

Extensive appendix material improves reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates for data augmentation, case studies with actual generated Verilog, and a sensitivity analysis across different PDKs/synthesis tools/optimization targets (Table 9), which strengthens claims that gains are not an artifact of one toolchain configuration.
A scalability study on larger AutoSilicon designs (~560 LoC, CPU/NPU blocks) provides some evidence the approach is not limited to small textbook RTLLM/VerilogEval tasks.
The runtime/acceleration analysis (fail-fast + parallel reward computation) is a useful practical contribution given how costly EDA-in-the-loop RL can be.
weaknesses: Relevance to the core NLP/computational-linguistics audience of ACL is questionable: the contribution is essentially an RL system engineering result for EDA/RTL generation (reward shaping, curriculum weighting, toolchain integration) with limited connection to language modeling, semantics, or other central CL concerns beyond using an LLM as the policy; the paper would fit more naturally in an EDA/ML-systems venue (DAC/ICCAD/MLSys) than an ACL track.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: ChipSeek is compared against RTLCoder, CodeV, Origen, CraftRTL, etc., which were trained on different (and possibly overlapping or non-overlapping) data, with different SFT corpora and different amounts of compute; it is unclear how much of the reported gain is attributable to CDPO/reward design versus simply having access to a stronger/more PPA-aware augmented dataset that competitors lack.

All quantitative results appear to be single-run point estimates with no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed reporting, despite RL training being known to be high-variance; this makes it hard to assess whether reported improvements (some of which are only a few points, e.g., VerilogEval Human pass@1) are robust or within noise.

The PPA reward formulation rm = ref_m/gen_m directly ties training reward to the specific reference designs and EDA flow (NanGate45/Yosys/OpenROAD) used to build the RL dataset; although a sensitivity study is provided, it only varies the evaluation-time toolchain, not the training-time reward computation, so a residual concern about overfitting to the specific reward-computation flow remains.

Some benchmark/table details are inconsistent or underspecified (e.g., Table 1 cites RTLLM v1.1 results attributed to Liu et al. 2024b, whose reference entry describes it as 'OpenLLM-RTL' rather than RTLLM v1.1; GPT-5 is used as a testbench generator, but its capabilities/version and potential contamination effects on the benchmark testbenches are not discussed), which reduces confidence in exact reproducibility of the pipeline.

The paper's central algorithmic novelty (decoupled/advantage-level aggregation of multiple reward heads plus an EMA-based curriculum coefficient) is a relatively incremental extension over GRPO/DAPO-style advantage normalization, and the ablations, while present, do not fully isolate whether gains come from the curriculum mechanism itself versus simply having more/better fine-grained reward signals available.

The optimization/failure analysis (Section 5) attributes weaker performance on Control/Memory modules to data scarcity but this is only a post-hoc hypothesis without further investigation or mitigation, leaving an important limitation largely unaddressed.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap in LLM-based RTL generation: existing SFT/RAG/agentic approaches optimize functional correctness but largely ignore PPA (power/performance/area), and the paper proposes a concrete closed-loop EDA-in-the-loop RL solution.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning VerilogEval (Machine/Human), RTLLM v1.1 and v2.0, four base models, fine-grained preference-conditioned PPA optimization, a scalability study on larger AutoSilicon designs, and a sensitivity analysis across multiple PDKs/synthesis tools/optimization targets, which is unusually thorough for this application area.

Reasonably detailed ablations isolating the contribution of each reward component (format/syntax/function/synthesis/PPA) and each CDPO design choice (advantage-level aggregation, curriculum schedule, preference vector), as well as a direct comparison against GRPO and DAPO baselines.

Practical engineering contributions (hierarchical gating/fail-fast filtering, parallelized reward computation) with quantified runtime savings, which matter for the feasibility of EDA-in-the-loop RL and aid reproducibility of the training pipeline.

Clear qualitative case study (barrel shifter) illustrating a plausible, interpretable mechanism (behavioral description enabling better synthesis-tool optimization) behind the PPA gains, rather than relying solely on aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty (CDPO) is incremental relative to existing RLVR/GRPO-style methods: decoupled per-component advantage normalization, curriculum-weighted scalarization, and preference-conditioned weighting are reasonable but fairly standard multi-objective RL reward-shaping techniques rather than a fundamentally new optimization method; the paper does not clearly differentiate CDPO from existing multi-reward RL approaches beyond the specific application.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting anywhere (main results, ablations, or RL training curves) despite RL being notoriously high-variance; all comparisons are single-run point estimates, which undermines confidence in claimed state-of-the-art margins, especially on the small RTLLM v2.0 benchmark (~44 designs).

The automated data augmentation pipeline (testbenches, reasoning traces, PPA-aware prompts) depends on proprietary commercial models (GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1) for generating training/eval artifacts; self-generated testbenches used as correctness oracles for reward computation raise concerns about systematic reward-signal errors (false positives/negatives) that are not analyzed, and reliance on closed models limits exact reproducibility.

Table 11's detailed per-design PPA comparison shows several functional failures (N/A entries, e.g., asyn_fifo, multi_pipe_8bit, radix2_div) and at least one case (freq_divbyodd) where ChipSeek is substantially worse on delay and area than the baseline despite being highlighted in a 'wins' table; these negative/mixed results are not discussed or analyzed in the text, suggesting selective emphasis on favorable outcomes.

Baselines (CodeV, CraftRTL, Origen, ReasoningV, RTLCoder) differ in base model, training data scale/source, and training recipe, so head-to-head 'state-of-the-art' claims are confounded by factors other than the proposed RL method; no controlled comparison isolates the effect of CDPO versus simply using more/better data.

Potential reward-hacking risks (e.g., trivial or degenerate but functionally-passing designs minimizing area/power, or testbenches with insufficient coverage inflating the function reward) are not discussed or empirically probed, which is an important soundness concern for an EDA-in-the-loop RL reward design.

Presentation is dense and symbol-heavy (Sections 3.2–3.3, Appendix A) with limited intuition given for several design choices (e.g., exact curriculum EMA dynamics, specific weighting constants), making it harder to assess sensitivity to hyperparameters not covered by the ablations shown.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and genuine gap: prior LLM-based RTL generation methods either optimize functional correctness via SFT (ignoring PPA) or apply external post-hoc optimization (not improving intrinsic model ability). The proposed EDA-integrated RL loop directly closes this gap.

The CDPO algorithm is a substantive methodological contribution with clear motivation: it explicitly targets two identified problems in multi-objective RLVR (learning-stage mismatch and reward-scale mismatch) via decoupled advantage normalization, an EMA-smoothed curriculum weight schedule, and preference-conditioned PPA weighting for controllable trade-offs.

Extensive empirical validation across four base models and multiple benchmarks (VerilogEval Machine/Human, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0, AutoSilicon large-scale designs), consistently outperforming strong recent baselines (CodeV, Origen, CraftRTL, RTLCoder, GPT-4o/o1).

Thorough ablations: individual reward-component removal, direct comparison of CDPO against GRPO and DAPO, training-stage (SFT vs SFT+CDPO) breakdown, and component-level ablation (advantage aggregation, curriculum, preference vector) all support the claimed mechanisms.

A dedicated sensitivity study across different PDKs, synthesis tools, and optimization strategies (Table 9) provides good evidence that improvements are not artifacts of a single toolchain configuration, strengthening the soundness of the PPA claims.

Good engineering/reproducibility detail: hierarchical gating for computational efficiency, explicit hyperparameters, prompt templates, and training infrastructure are documented, aiding reproducibility despite the complex pipeline.
Illustrative case study (barrel shifter) provides qualitative insight into what kind of optimization behavior (operator inference) the model learns, complementing the quantitative results.
weaknesses: No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the main comparisons despite RL training being known to be high-variance; single-run numbers make some of the reported gains (e.g., small percentage differences in ablations) harder to assess as statistically robust.

The functional-correctness reward critically depends on LLM-generated testbenches (via an unspecified/ambiguous 'GPT-5' model); testbench quality and coverage are not independently validated, so noise or gaps in reward signal could silently bias training or evaluation results.

PPA reward is defined relative to a fixed reference design (rm = refm/genm); the paper does not discuss how reference-design quality/optimality was ensured, leaving open whether some gains reflect weak reference baselines rather than genuinely superior designs.

Discussion of the weaker performance on Control and Memory modules is limited to a plausible but unverified hypothesis (training data scarcity) without deeper diagnostic analysis or targeted experiments.

Some strongly related PPA-optimization baselines discussed in the related work (RTLRewriter, SymRTLO) are not included in the main quantitative comparison tables, limiting the completeness of the empirical comparison against the most directly competing post-hoc optimization methods.

The paper's relevance to core computational linguistics is indirect—this is fundamentally an EDA/RL-for-code-generation contribution; its fit to ACL's core NLP audience, while acceptable under the code-generation/LLM application umbrella, is narrower than typical main-conference NLP contributions.

Presentation of the CDPO formalism (Section 3.3) is dense and notation-heavy, which could hinder accessibility for readers not deeply familiar with RLVR/GRPO-style methods; clearer intuition-first exposition would improve clarity.
